newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia at crossroads, seen needing new econ policy.
newsitem.headline: Croatia at crossroads, seen needing new econ policy.

text.p: Croatia is at an economic crossroads and badly needs a new, consistent economic policy and development strategy in 1997, Friday's newspapers quoted leading economists as saying at their annual conference.
A pivotal problem is how to start a new investment cycle, daily Vecernji List reported Vladimir Veselica, head of the economists' association, as telling the gathering.
The government has succeeded in stabilising prices and exchange rate of the domestic currency, the kuna, through a harsh austerity programme in the past three years.

But economist Branimir Lokin was reported by another daily Vjesnik to have blamed the kuna's strong rate for making Croatian products less competitive abroad, costing exporters at least a $200 million loss so far this year.
Spurred by an industrial recovery and return of foreign tourists since the end of conflicts in former Yugoslavia in 1995, the economy has also begun to pick up.
However, Veselica described a constant shrinkage of the share of agriculture and industry as "worrisome", while only services were expanding.

He said a revival that could produce a desired 10-12 percent rise in the country's gross national product over the next few years hinged on heavier investments into the ailing primary and secondary sector.
Croatia's gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to rise between five and seven percent in real terms this year. Officials predict it will grow 9.3 percent nominally in 1997.
While the banks, which badly need restructuring, lack cash to power such a boom, economists said the country would rely on foreign funding for some time to come.

Still Lokin warned as huge amounts of money flowed into pure consumption scarse resources would prevent even the foreign loans being successfully transferred into kuna for investments. -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075
